factual_errors.claim: "First check the converter's mode" as a way to resolve DH-485 comms via the USR-N540
factual_errors.why_wrong: A transparent RS-485-Ethernet bridge has no protocol-aware mode that adds DH-485 token-passing/TX-EN support; there is no mode setting that makes it DH-485-capable, so this framing risks sending the technician down a dead end before the real fix.

factual_errors.claim: "[Source: Rockwell Automation CompactLogix — Communication]" is cited for the causal claim that the USR-N540 lacks DH-485 protocol handling
factual_errors.why_wrong: The retrieved excerpt never mentions the USR-N540 or explains why transparent converters fail on DH-485 — it only shows wiring a 1761-NET-AIC. The citation only supports the remedy, not the stated cause.

factual_errors.claim: No mention of the DH-485 0-5V RS-485 vs. Ethernet voltage mismatch
factual_errors.why_wrong: This is a documented equipment-damage risk when the wrong converter type is connected; omitting it is a real gap even though the answer's remedy is otherwise correct.

notes: Excerpt 1 (CompactLogix DH-485 manual) genuinely supports the fix: it shows a 1761-NET-AIC converter and an SLC 5/03 on a DH-485 network, so recommending 1761-NET-AIC is grounded. Excerpt 2 is an unrelated VFD network I/O map and supports nothing here. MIRA's causal claim ('USR-N540 is transparent, lacks DH-485 protocol handling') is not stated anywhere in the excerpts — plausible inference, but tagged with a citation that doesn't actually cover it. 'Check the converter's mode' is a soft hedge that could mislead, since no mode fixes DH-485 incompatibility. No mention of token-passing arbitration, TX-EN control line, half-duplex turnaround, or the RS-485/Ethernet voltage mismatch. Net: better than a prior graded version (states the correct remedy directly) but still under-grounded on the 'why' and missing a known damage-risk warning.
